source.title: The Local Interaction Basis: Identifying Computationally-Relevant and Sparsely Interacting Features in Neural Networks
source.authors: Lucius Bushnaq; S. Heimersheim; Nicholas Goldowsky-Dill; Dan Braun; Jake Mendel; Kaarel Hänni; Avery Griffin; Jörn Stöhler; Magdalena Wache; Marius Hobbhahn

record.tranche_reason: The study qualitatively checks whether interpretations suggested by activating examples generalize to other activations, and reports cases where they do not; this refines the claim that apparent interpretability from examples can overstate what is explained.
record.gate_note: The paper's discussion of neuron polysemanticity and cited examples are background, not results from its own experiments. Its own language-model results inspect LIB directions rather than neuron poles; it does not report neuron-pole shares or automated explanation scores. The counted results are qualitative checks of whether example-based interpretations predict activations beyond the examples that suggested them.
record.test_reason: The paper builds an alternative basis (LIB) and inspects LIB and PCA directions in GPT2-small, not individual neurons. Its activating-example checks concern basis directions, so they do not measure what V6 names: explanations of a neuron's firing. Neuron polysemanticity appears only as cited background motivating the method. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right but incomplete. The main conclusion is that LIB yields more computationally relevant, sparser features than PCA on toy models (modular addition, CIFAR-10 MLP), but on language models it gives only modest sparsity gains, no better interpretability than PCA, and no modularity. The authors speculate the assumption of a linear non-overcomplete basis fails for LMs. The caution that top-activating-sample interpretations may not predict intermediate activations is a secondary remark.
record.recipe_differences: The paper develops and evaluates a Local Interaction Basis and integrated-gradient interaction graphs, comparing LIB with PCA. The qualitative activation-example inspection is not the Qwen3 neuron-pole audit or an automated explanation-scoring procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper notes that interpretations based on maximum and minimum activating examples may fail on intermediate-activation examples; it suggests custom prompts and more intermediate samples as possible improvements, but does not test those alternatives.

fits_no_version.finding: In GPT2-small block 6, interpretations suggested by max/min activating examples of LIB directions (105, 109, 304) fail to explain intermediate-activation examples. Features 82 and 477 have no clear interpretation. PCA directions are described as similarly uninterpretable.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For non-neuron basis directions (LIB/PCA) in a small LM, explanations drawn from top-activating examples often fail to predict intermediate activations.

record.problems: The evidence relevant to V6 is qualitative inspection of selected features and dataset examples, with no systematic held-out predictive score or uncertainty estimate. The authors note that a detailed interpretability analysis is out of scope.
record.rows_left_out: No results on neuron-pole job shares, InceptionV1, attribution graphs built from neurons, or automated explanation scoring were reported as experiments relevant to the listed versions. The paper's edge-ablation and language-model sparsity results measure interaction sparsity rather than the example-based explanation failure in V6.

untested.parts: No audit of Qwen3-32B neuron poles or job shares.
No neuron-level audit across models or scale.
No analysis of InceptionV1 or of canonical polysemantic neurons.
No estimate of interpretable-neuron shares, and no test of architecture or tool effects on neurons.
Interaction graphs are built in the LIB/PCA basis, not the model's own neurons; no comparison with replacement models.
No neuron explanations are checked against held-out activations; only LIB directions are inspected.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked LIB-direction inspections to V6, but V6 concerns neuron explanations; the subjects here are learned basis directions. The paper's only neuron-related content is cited background on polysemanticity.

versions.untested_parts: No audit of Qwen3-32B neuron poles or estimate of the shares with one, two, or unknown jobs.
No cross-model or scale audit of neuron-pole job shares.
Does not analyze InceptionV1's cat-and-car neuron or test the pose interpretation.
Does not estimate interpretable-neuron shares for InceptionV1-sized vision models or test whether architecture, regularization, or tools cause the proposed increase.
The paper builds interaction graphs in a transformed basis; it does not test whether attribution graphs using a large model's own neurons explain behavior without a replacement model.
The evidence is qualitative inspection of selected GPT2-small LIB directions and activation examples, not a systematic held-out test across neurons or models.
No automated scoring by simulating explanation-predicted activations on new text, or good-score rate.

rows.subject: GPT2-small
rows.operation_detail: Inspected examples at different activation levels for LIB feature 105 and checked whether the proposed last-name/brand-name interpretation fit them.
rows.measure: Whether the interpretation suggested by highly activating examples accounts for examples at other activation levels.
rows.value: The feature seemed to activate on first tokens of last names and brand names, but other samples did not follow that rule.
rows.note: A qualitative inspection; the authors describe the proposed interpretation as imperfect.
rows.check: Subject is LIB direction 105, a rotated and whitened basis direction, not a neuron pole. The finding is an example-based interpretation that fits only imperfectly; it does not bear on V6's neuron-level claim.

source_check.problem: Fine as extracted. The text calls feature 105 'somewhat interpretable' and notes samples that break the rule. Subject is a LIB direction, not a neuron, so versions none is right.

rows.subject: GPT2-small
rows.operation_detail: Inspected examples at different activation levels for LIB feature 109 and checked whether the top-example interpretation accounted for intermediate activations.
rows.measure: Whether the interpretation suggested by top-activating examples predicts activations in other samples.
rows.value: Top examples included “Hawk” in a graphics-card name and surnames beginning with H; minimally activating examples included “cos” and similar tokens. These interpretations did not explain intermediate-activation examples.
rows.note: The authors state that the top-sample interpretation was not predictive and was likely incorrect.
rows.check: Subject is LIB direction 109, not a neuron. The authors say the top-sample interpretation is not predictive of intermediate activations, but for a basis direction, not a neuron.

source_check.problem: Fine. The text says the top-sample interpretation is 'not predictive and likely not correct'. It is a basis direction, so it does not link to V6.

relation.reason: The intro argues from cited work that the neuron basis is not the right unit because of polysemanticity. The paper has no results of its own on neurons, so the reader's 'tests' call is not supported.

tranche.reason: The paper compares LIB and PCA bases on basis directions and never evaluates the neuron basis. Neuron polysemanticity appears only as cited background in the intro, so it neither tests nor uses any version. The reader's T5 call is not supported.

source_check.notes: All three rows are LIB directions in GPT2-small (85M), not neurons, so none bears on V6 or any other version. The failure of top-example interpretations (features 109, 304) is analogous to V6 but applies to rotated basis directions. No verdicts are warranted.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Qualitative inspections of GPT2-small LIB features 109 and 304; feature 105 shows a weaker instance
reader_labels.reason: Suggested interpretations failed to account for other activation examples for features 109 and 304, and fit feature 105 only imperfectly (R1–R3).
